content: A headache is defined as a condition characterized by pain localized to the head. In some cases, pain in the neck or upper back may also be perceived as a headache. It is one of the most frequently reported complaints of localized pain. The historical understanding of headaches dates back to 1672, when Thomas Willis published a classification system in De Cephalalgia that bears resemblance to modern categorizations. Later, in 1787, Christian Baur introduced a broader classification, dividing headaches into two main categories: idiopathic (now referred to as primary headaches) and symptomatic (secondary headaches). He further identified 84 distinct types of headaches. From a pathophysiological perspective, the brain itself is not capable of perceiving pain, as it lacks pain-sensitive nerve fibers. However, pain can arise from various structures in the head, including a network of nerves that extend across the scalp, as well as certain nerves in the face, mouth, and throat. The meninges (the protective layers surrounding the brain) and blood vessels are capable of perceiving pain. Headaches are often caused by traction or irritation of these meninges and blood vessels. Additionally, the muscles of the head can also be sensitive to pain, contributing to headache symptoms. The majority of headaches are benign and self-limiting. Common causes include tension, neck pain, migraines, eye strain, dehydration, low blood sugar, and sinusitis. Chronic headaches are often multifactorial in origin. However, in rare cases, headaches may be caused by life-threatening conditions such as meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral aneurysms, severe hypertension, or brain tumors. When a headache occurs following a head injury, the cause is usually apparent. In women, a significant proportion of headaches are linked to hormonal fluctuations in estrogen levels during the menstrual cycle. These headaches may occur before, during, or even in the middle of the menstrual cycle. The prognosis of a headache largely depends on its underlying cause. In terms of diagnostic evaluation, laboratory tests may assist in narrowing down the differential diagnosis, but they are rarely definitive for identifying specific types of headaches. Imaging studies, such as computed tomography (CT) scans of the brain or sinuses, are commonly utilized. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and sinuses is performed in specific clinical scenarios to provide further diagnostic clarity. Treatment of headaches often involves medical therapies, including the use of analgesics. In certain cases, more advanced approaches, such as the implantation of electrodes, may be employed. Preventative strategies are also available for some types of headaches, such as migraines, which may respond to prophylactic treatments.
